draft.briefing: Hey, you're at Shaniwar Wada! Built in 1732, this was the seat of the Peshwas of the Maratha Confederacy until 1818. In 1828 most of it burned down in a fire nobody has ever explained, and what survived is what you see today.
draft.hungryLine: You're in the old Peth area, which is misal country, so go for a plate of spicy misal at one of the famous local joints if you can take the heat.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Kasba Ganapati, Pune's presiding deity, is a 3 min walk. Appa Balwant Chowk with its bookshops is 5 minutes, and Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple is 6 minutes away.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Wander over to Appa Balwant Chowk, known as ABC, and browse the bookshops packed around the crossroads.
moodReplies.surprise-me: The main idol at Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple is insured for ₹10 million.

spots.name: Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple
spots.detail: 6 min walk · Pune's best known Ganesha temple, huge during Ganeshotsav

legends.title: A Ganesha the size of a grain
legends.body: Locals say the Kasba Ganapati idol is self-made and was once as small as a grain of rice. It has grown because of a coating of red sandalwood.

tips.title: Plan around Ganeshotsav.
tips.body: Around September, the ten-day Ganesh festival leaves the old city's inner streets almost blocked, so expect crowds and slow going.

tips.title: Take the metro in.
tips.body: PMC Bhavan metro station on the Aqua Line is a 7 min walk, and its design is inspired by the old wadas of the peths.

story.title: Many rulers
story.body: Before the Peshwas, Pune was ruled at different times by the Rashtrakutas, the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, the Mughals and the Adil Shahis. This ward, Shaniwar Peth, was once known as Murtuzabad.

story.title: Home of the Peshwas
story.body: Shaniwar Wada was built in 1732 and became the seat of the Peshwas, the prime ministers of the Maratha Confederacy, until 1818.

story.title: The last Peshwa
story.body: Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa, lived at Vishrambaug Wada, a 20,000 sq ft mansion famous for its carved wooden balcony. Today it holds a post office and a small museum of Maratha artifacts.

story.title: The great fire
story.body: In 1828 an unexplained fire destroyed most of Shaniwar Wada. The structures that survived are now kept as a tourist site.

story.title: The old city lives on
story.body: Around the wada, the peths still buzz with temples, bookshops and Ganesh mandals. The PMC Bhavan metro station, opened in 2023, even borrows its look from the wadas.
